newsitem.title: UK: Base metals and gold slump as buyers stay away.
newsitem.headline: Base metals and gold slump as buyers stay away.

text.p: World prices for industrial metals took another dive on Tuesday as consumers around the globe backed off and waited for lower values.
With order books emptier than they had expected earlier in 1996, they can afford to live hand-to-mouth, analysts said.
"Most economies still appear to be bedevilled by high raw material stocks as well as finished product inventories," said Robin Bhar of London Metal Exchange (LME) ring dealers Brandeis.
"The consumers' own order levels are not that strong."
Gold prices hit their lowest level in 18 months with analysts saying consumer were reluctance to buy until they were convinced the price had reached a floor.
On the LME prices for aluminium fell to 2-1/4 year lows, lead slumped to a fresh seven-month nadir, tin was its weakest for sixteen months and nickel fell to a two-month low.
The flagship copper contract extended recent sharp losses to around $100 from late last week to $1,890 and only zinc showed a semblance of stability.
The woeful performance came on the first day of the last quarter of 1996, traditionally the strongest period for demand following the seasonal summer slowdown.
On Tuesday values were hit by speculator and fund sales.

"To some extent it is a pure sentiment play," said one floor dealer. "People want to sell copper and that spills over everywhere else. If you are going to play the market you play it from the short side."
This week's losses came despite a three-percent fall in LME copper stocks on Tuesday of 7,825 tonnes.
Aluminium, used by the packaging and transportation industries, hit a 2-1/4 year low of $1,357 from $1,377.50 on Monday after stocks fell by a modest 950 tonnes.
Hopes early this year that gold prices would soar have been crumbling for weeks and reached their deepest trough yet when bullion hit an 18-month low.
"Negative sentiment has been building up for a while," one analyst said after gold was fixed at $377.05 per ounce, its lowest official fixing since March 6 last year.
The previous day it was set at $379.00 and a month ago it was a relatively healthy $386.90, but still well off the $416.25 set at the peak of a blistering five-week rally on February 2.
The agricultural commodites had a mixed day with coffee rebounding after lower-than-forecast certified coffee stock figures were issued from New York late on Monday.
However cocoa and sugar were both quiet with the former slipping on the basis of rumours the Ivorian crop would be larger than initially forecast.
Grains prices were generally lower as well led by the Chicago board of Trade soybean futures which were sold by the investment funds on good weather and crop ratings reports.
